speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In brief, a statutory declaration is a written statement that a person signs and solemnly declares to be true.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Making a false statutory declaration is a serious criminal offence.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For example, producing a false statutory declaration to a Court can result in a jail term of up to seven years.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Apart from use in Court proceedings, statutory declarations may also be taken for a myriad of commercial or regulatory purposes, such as registering a ship, declaring that a company is solvent, transferring a bill of sale or affirming that contractual obligations have been complied with.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Some public agencies may also require certain applications to be supported by a statutory declaration.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For instance, applications to the Registrar of Titles for a replacement Certificate of Title must be accompanied by a statutory declaration setting out the circumstances leading to the loss of the original Certificate.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Given the weight that can be placed on facts set out in a sworn statutory declaration and the serious consequences associated with making a false statutory declaration, the law today requires a statutory declaration to be made in a specific form and manner.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Therefore, a statutory declaration must take the form that is set out in the Oaths and Declarations Act.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And it must also be made before an authorised person, such as a Commissioner for Oaths, or CFO for short, who will check the identity of the declarant and ensure that the declarant is aware of what he is doing and aware of the consequences of making a false declaration.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Next, an oath or affirmation is a solemn declaration by which a person swears or affirms that what he says is the truth or that he will do as he has promised to do.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There is a wide range of circumstances in which a person may be required to take an oath, but most oaths fall within two broad categories.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: First, a person, such as a witness, may be required to take an oath before giving evidence, for example, to a Court or tribunal.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Second, a person may also be required to take an oath if he or she is appointed to an office, such as that of a Judge.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For example, before assuming office, Supreme Court Judges are required under the Constitution to solemnly swear to faithfully discharge their judicial duties and do right without fear or favour.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Last, I come to notarial functions that are performed by a Notary Public in Singapore, or NP for short.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: From time to time, individuals or businesses may need to obtain a notarial act from a NP.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For example, an individual may need a certified true copy of an original document such as his identity card or academic certificate to apply to a foreign educational institution for further studies; or a business may need a NP to witness the due execution of a document that is meant for use overseas.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The process of obtaining a notarial act is a stringent one.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Notaries must keep a full and accurate record of the whole procedure.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Further, each notarial certificate issued by the NP is serialised and must be presented to the Singapore Academy of Law for authentication.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This mitigates the risk of forgery, safeguards the integrity of the process and provides foreign recipients with the assurance that they need in order to rely on documents that are notarised by a NP in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Further, the process is often paper-based, involving the use of wet ink signatures.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These requirements all help to ensure the integrity of the process – for the reasons I have outlined earlier.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It is now possible with the touch of a button to see and hear, through video-conferencing software, a person who is on the other end of Singapore – something unthinkable when these requirements were first formulated centuries ago.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Society is also increasingly comfortable with relying on digital processes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This is in line with the Government’s ongoing efforts to facilitate electronic transactions, by progressively reviewing and updating the relevant legal frameworks in place.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The first aspect is that of electronic meetings with authorised service providers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Bill sets out certain minimum requirements relating to the quality of such electronic means of communication.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And we also intend to prescribe further procedural requirements or safeguards that parties must comply with, in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Board of Commissioners for Oaths and Notaries Public under the Singapore Academy of Law also intends to issue refreshed guidelines that will assist CFOs and NPs in carrying out their functions under this framework.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We understand that these guidelines will include guidance on the circumstances in which it may be inappropriate for a CFO or NP to provide their services remotely.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In some cases, such as oaths of office that are taken by officeholders under the Constitution or other Acts, the Bills will make clarificatory amendments so as to provide for greater legal certainty.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The second aspect is that of electronic signing.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As a safeguard for statutory declarations, it will be necessary to only use the type of electronic signature that will be prescribed in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In deciding the type of electronic signature to prescribe in subsidiary legislation, we will consider factors, such as performance standards, security, reliability and ease of access for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For notarial acts or oaths that must be subscribed with a signature – such as oaths administered in the course of judicial proceedings, or oaths taken by officeholders under the Constitution – the Constitution (Amendment) Bill, and the Oaths, Declarations and Notarisations (Remote Methods) Bill do not change the position in relation to how these should be signed.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Notarial acts or oaths arise in a variety of situations, with different needs and circumstances.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We will, therefore, leave the precise signing requirements to be determined by the relevant sectorial agency.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Before I conclude, Mr Speaker, let me touch on a couple of points.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The first point is that the framework is enabling and not prescriptive.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It provides individuals, businesses and service providers with an electronic option, for the various legal processes that I have spoken of.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The framework does not require or mandate the use of such electronic options.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This means that the public can continue with their existing in-person and/or paper-based processes if they wish.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It follows that the legislative framework does not oblige Government agencies, a Commissioner for Oath or a Notary Public to provide or adopt an electronic option.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For example, public agencies administer or require the taking of statutory declarations or oaths in a wide variety of circumstances.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There may be important, or simply practical, reasons for physical processes to continue.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It may be that certain oaths of office or other Constitutional oaths continue to be taken in person as a general rule because of the gravity and solemnity associated with such oaths.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In other cases, it may be that the agency in question has some specific policy or practical reason to require a person’s physical presence when taking a statutory declaration or oath.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The second point relates to statutory declarations and notarial acts that have already been made in a process that involved remote witnessing.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For example, this may have been done during the COVID-19 pandemic when movement restrictions were in place.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This should address concerns around the validity of statutory declarations or notarial acts made in a process involving remote witnessing before this Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The validation clauses under the Oaths, Declarations and Notarisations (Remote Methods) Bill apply only to those statutory declarations and notarial acts that were done using a live video or live television link.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, for example, a statutory declaration or notarial act that was done only by telephone will not be validated.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The validation clauses also do not affect a person’s right to challenge the validity of a statutory declaration or notarial act on the basis that some other requirement, apart from the in-person witnessing requirement, was not met.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The framework I have just outlined is crafted to strike a balance between convenience and efficiency on the one hand and safeguarding the integrity of the process on the other hand.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Bills have also been designed to be as technology neutral as possible, with details devolved to subsidiary legislation, so that the framework and its associated safeguards can be updated from time to time to keep pace with technological developments.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This would enhance convenience, efficiency and accessibility for the oath takers and the oath administrators.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, I seek a few clarifications in two broad areas: authentication and contingencies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In particular, will there be other means of verifying their identity and authenticity?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we ensure that the feed is adequately fast, clear and secure for the oaths to be taken smoothly?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Notwithstanding, we must be mindful of the potential challenges and risks involved, given the increasing sophistication of deep fake AI technology.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.45 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.24 pm until 4.45 pm.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I have also spoken to fellow legal practitioners who are currently notaries and commissioners for oaths in the course of preparing for my speech.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Section 4A provides that such electronic means of communication should allow the notaries to (a) communicate with the person who is executing the documents or making an oath or affirmation, as well as any witness or interpreter present; (b) confirm the identity of the relevant person and any witness or interpreter; and (c) verify by inspection any document to be signed or sworn.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The new section 4A(3) also allows notaries to rely on any electronic means of communication created by remote communication technology as allowed under this Bill in the course of issuing a notarial certificate of the nature and the authenticity of a particular document.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In fact, the rules for Commissioner for Oaths were pragmatically altered to allow Commissioners for Oath to do the commissioning of affidavits via video conferencing.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: During such online commissioning, Commissioners for Oaths are required to verify through visual inspection, via video conference of the deponent and his or her identity document, and that the deponent is who he or she said she is.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The rules also require, among other things, the Commissioner to maintain visual contact with the deponent during the commissioning or executing process, and in effect, confirm that the deponent has signed the same document.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I recall that it was challenging for many notaries to perform notarial work during COVID-19, especially in the early days of COVID-19, even though there was still demand for such work.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Notarisations were still required, especially for documents to be used abroad for a variety of reasons, notwithstanding COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A variety of business, legal and even personal transactions still had to be performed, requiring notaries to assist with the execution of documents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: During the circuit breaker days, not all notaries were officially allowed – at least initially – to do their work in their offices.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Arranging notarial appointments can be physically challenging, even when the work was legitimate and necessary.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The proposed changes in this Bill would have provided good options for notaries, even as the proposed changes still have some inherent challenges which I will discuss briefly below.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I will call this other person who is executing a document, "the relevant person", for the remaining part of my speech.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The notary will need to look at the original identification documents of such a person, often keeping a copy of such documents for records purposes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, for foreigners who come with their foreign passports as proof of identity, especially coming to see the notaries for the first time or on a one-off basis, notaries often have no choice but to give the benefit of doubt that the passports are genuine, even if they have no idea what the passport should even look like or if it is authentic.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Similarly, when clients come in with what they claim to be original documents for notaries to certify copies of such documents, notaries will not always be in a position to ascertain on the spot whether such documents are genuine or fake.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: They have to take the word of the client that they are genuine and notarise a certified true copy of it.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The above are already the common experiences of notaries prior to the proposed amendments, which we are looking at today.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I think the new amendments allowing notaries to notarise via a live video link may in some cases make it even more difficult for a notary to verify the relevant person's identity, when executing documents before a notary via video link, or to verify the authenticity of documents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is especially as the notary is not familiar with the relevant person, and it is not easy to cite and verify the identification document or the documents which are the subject of notarial acts by just looking at the screen.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The notary does not even get to touch or flip the documents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Some practitioners also shared with me that for online commissioning of affidavits, they may have the added reassurance that the clients or deponents were introduced by their own lawyers who helped to prepare the affidavits and these lawyers may be personally known to the Commissioners for Oaths or have regularly brought their clients to the same Commissioner for Oaths for affirmation of oaths.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This may not be the case for much of the notarial work.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is not necessarily easy to determine whether a relevant person is in Singapore or not when a notarial transaction is being performed online.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It will certainly be easier to require physical meeting with a client.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In short, it will not be easy for the notary to always avoid any fraudulent attempts on the part of the relevant person in some of the aspects that I have discussed above.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Some practitioners may understandably be concerned, that as a matter of professional liability, their conclusions regarding the identity, the whereabouts of the relevant person or even regarding the authenticity of the documents in question are later contradicted by subsequent evidence coming to light after that.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But the relatively low fees they are supposed to charge as required by the authorities as compared to the fees of notaries in civil law countries, or to even the usual hourly charges lawyers may charge for other types of work.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It may not be fair for notaries to bear the risk of having to ascertain certain facts when it would not be cost-effective or even fully plausible for them to do so.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is interesting to note that the COVID-19 guidance on remote notarisation document in the United Kingdom (UK) provide some useful protection for the notary in the areas we have discussed.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such provisions, by way of example, will give fair protection to notaries.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope that the authorities can incorporate similar guidelines in any subsidiary legislation or rules for notaries.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Of course, such penalties will require further changes to the law.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope that the authorities will take cognisance of the risk and issues raised and will not accord an impractically high standard of care on notaries in expecting them to be professionally liable, should the identity of the relevant persons or the location of the relevant persons or even the authenticity of the original documents provided be subject to a deliberate misrepresentation of fraudulent conduct on a part of the relevant person themselves.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Assuming of course that the verifications of identity are done appropriately, and the administration is properly done online with unblocked line of sight, allowing such commissioning en mass online may truly capitalise the capability of e-communication means to reach many deponents all at once.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope that the authorities will not impose an impractically high and onerous standard of care expected of practitioners in complying with the new provisions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I do take note that the Senior Parliamentary Secretary has highlighted that this will not be prescriptive.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I also support the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore (Amendment No 2) Bill.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I am also a Commissioner of Oath and a Notary Public.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The role of a Commissioner of Oath is set up in section 68 of the Supreme Court of Judicature Act 1969.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Broadly speaking, a Commissioner for Oath administers oaths for any affidavit or affirmation, swear executors and administrators, and take and receive statutory declarations.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The role of a Notary Public is set up in a Notaries Public Act 1959.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Members of the public will usually associate a notary public as a senior lawyer who is called upon to certify documents for use overseas or to administer any oath or affirmation in connection with any affidavit or statutory declaration which is used in any court or place outside Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Statutory declarations and affidavits are required by law for a number of legal and business matters.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Under various regulations in Singapore, an applicant may be required to make certain statutory declarations and affidavits for the purposes of their business or tax-related matters.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For correlated matters, deponents are required to swear or affirm affidavits for use in Court.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: As making false oath in Court proceedings and making false statutory declarations is an offence, the deponent would usually have to appear before a Commissioner for Oaths to enable the commissioner to verify the deponent's identity and to ensure that the deponent understands the contents of the document that they are signing.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In a case where the affidavit or declaration is for use in an overseas court, the notary public performs a similar function.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: During the COVID-19 pandemic, the Ministry of Health (MOH) had introduced various measures like the circuit breaker, heightened alert, social distancing and work-from-home so as to break the chain of viral transmission.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, despite the COVID-19 pandemic, businesses need to continue to operate.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Life has to go on for many people.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This has affected the legal processes because businesses still need their staff to swear or affirm affidavits for Court proceedings.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Companies still need their senior management to sign documents before a Notary Public for use overseas; sometimes for incorporation of businesses overseas, sometimes, to sign reports for the purposes of reporting to regulatory authorities overseas.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: As a Commissioner for Oaths and a Notary Public, I had received many queries from deponents to ask whether they are allowed to affirm and sign affidavits, statutory declarations or other documents without physically being present before me.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Deponents and applicants point to the fact that they are having meetings and discussions via electronic modes of communications like Microsoft Teams and via Zoom.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There were also regulations which encouraged listed and unlisted companies to conduct their general meetings via electronic means.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This is to keep physical interactions and COVID-19 transmission risk to a minimum, which remain important in the long term even as safe distancing regulations have now been eased.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is no longer the same as 20 years ago, when you can only rely on expensive telephone calls to keep in touch with overseas relatives or friends.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I know of many parents who video call their children studying overseas on a regular basis to chat with them.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In the past, businessmen would rely on Skype or FaceTime video calls to carry out their meetings.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Today, we have WhatsApp, WeChat, Teams and Zoom video conferencing platforms, just to mention a few.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We should allow documents to be signed virtually so that in the event of future crises, where we are required to stay away from the office, we would still be able to function effectively using video technology.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I just wish to seek two clarifications from the Senior Parliamentary Secretary.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Save for the above two clarifications, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I support the various amendments to the Constitution and other Acts to allow for the administration of oaths through virtual means.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This move away from paper-based processes will bring time and cost savings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three clarifications on the safeguards for the framework.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first clarification is on the interpreter's involvement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Interpretation adds another step in the communication process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This can contribute to additional complexity if done over video link.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The risk of miscommunication may be higher for cases where specialised interpretation is needed, for example, for persons with special needs or disabilities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If the interpreter is allowed to be present over video link, can the Senior Parliamentary Secretary share what steps the Commissioner or Notary Public should take to ensure that the interpretation and communication is accurately done?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on the responsibility of a Commissioner or Notary Public to verify the independence of a client.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The risk of clients making oaths or affirmations under undue pressure is always present, even in in-person affirmations or notarisations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, where the Commissioner or Notary Public is only able to observe the client over video link, the risk is higher.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Parliamentary Secretary share what steps a Commissioner or Notary Public should take to ensure that the client signs any documents independently and without any undue pressure?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, must a Commissioner or Notary Public take additional steps to verify the persons in the room with the client and the relationships of these persons with the client?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Relatedly, can the Senior Parliamentary Secretary elaborate on the circumstances where a Commissioner or Notary Public should decline to take the oath or affirmation over video link?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My last point is on the security of communication links.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Parliamentary Secretary share whether there will be any requirements on the security of the platforms that will be permitted?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, must the platforms have end-to-end encryption to protect the video transmission?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Allowing remote oaths, affirmations or notarisations may open up a new avenue for scammers to solicit personal data.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Are there any methods in which clients can easily identify if the video links for oaths, affirmations or notarisations are valid?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: First, Mr Dennis Tan asked whether the amendments to section 11 apply to Commissioners for Oaths (CFOs), administering statutory declarations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Next, Mr Yip Hon Weng asked how we can guard against fraud and impersonation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Louis Ng asked what steps CFOs and Notary Publics (NPs) should take to ensure that the client is not under undue pressure over video link.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Dennis Tan commented that the use of electronic means of communication may come with some difficulties and asked that we do not increase the standard of care expected of CFOs and NPs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As I mentioned during my opening speech, the need to ensure the continuing integrity of the various processes was a key consideration when developing the electronic framework.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The possibility of fraud, impersonation and undue pressure is not unique to the electronic space.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Identity fraud and forgery can happen in the real world.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: To guard against this, the Singapore Academy of Law (SAL) has existing guidelines which advise CFOs and NPs to take steps to verify the identity of the person before them, for example, by requiring the person to produce a photo ID.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Nonetheless, we recognise that the adoption of technology introduces new ways in which fraud can be carried out.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Impersonation through deepfakes, which Mr Yip has mentioned, is one possibility that we need to be on our guard against.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: One requirement is that the electronic link must enable the person who is administering the oath or statutory declaration to confirm the identity of the client.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Further requirements may also be prescribed in subsidiary legislation under the Oaths, Declarations and Notarisations (Remote Methods) Bill, or the ODN Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These requirements can be reviewed and updated from time to time to keep pace with technological developments and to address new ways of committing fraud.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We will also work with the Singapore Academy of Law to update the existing guidelines for CFOs and NPs, so that the CFOs and NPs are equipped with the practical know-how to conduct transactions in a secure electronic environment.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: When formulating the revised guidelines, we will bear in mind the issues of fraud and impersonation which Mr Yip has raised.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We will also bear in mind the need to guard against undue influence.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: With this in mind, CFOs and NPs will likely be required to verify whether there are any other persons in the room with the client, and if so, who they are – a step that Mr Ng had alluded to and a step which CFOs are required to take today when commissioning affidavits remotely.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: All this being said, laws and guidelines are not in themselves sufficient.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Those who are entrusted with the responsibility to administer the oath or statutory declaration must continue to be vigilant and to take the necessary steps to satisfy themselves of the identity of the person taking the oath or making the statutory declaration and that the person is not under undue influence.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: With regard to Mr Dennis Tan's point on keeping to the existing standard of care, the revised requirements and guidelines are unlikely to result in significant additional burden to CFOs and NPs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Any specific requirements that are put in place will be those that are necessary to safeguard the integrity of the various processes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In a related vein, Mr Ng asked whether there are methods by which clients can verify if the video links for oaths, affirmations and notarisations are valid, rather than a scam.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The best defence against scams is a vigilant and discerning public.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Members of the public should take care to verify that the service provider they are engaging is legitimate and is not a scammer.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In this regard, the public can visit the SAL's website today to check whether a person is indeed a CFO or NP.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As with the use of any other online service, members of the public who wish to conduct transactions remotely should also keep a lookout for tell-tale signs of scams.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For example, they should check that any links that they receive are sent from the email address of the CFO or NP that they have been communicating with, and that the links point to an established video conferencing platform.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: If in doubt, members of the public should verify the authenticity of any links received through a separate channel such as a phone call with the CFO or NP.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Yip asked about the reliability of the electronic link and what happens if the electronic link is disrupted.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Ng also asked whether there are any requirements as to the security of the permitted platforms and whether, for instance, they must be secured with end-to-end encryption.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Bills are not prescriptive of the specific electronic platform that parties must use or how fast, clear or secure the electronic link must be.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Instead, the Bills set out broad outcomes that the electronic link must be capable of achieving.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: An electronic link will not meet these minimum requirements if it is of such poor quality that the service provider is unable to properly make out the client's face, or if it keeps dropping such that parties are unable to communicate properly.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In such cases, parties will have to try again with a better connection, or fall back to an in-person meeting.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As for the security of the electronic platform, it is up to the client and service provider to agree on an electronic platform that both are comfortable with using and that will best safeguard the confidentiality of the transaction.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The client may also request for an in-person meeting instead.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I should add that even in the absence of technical difficulties or concerns about confidentiality, it will still be open to any party to end the remote session at any time and request for an in-person meeting.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For instance, the service provider may do this if he or she feels that something is amiss.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Next, Mr Yip asked whether an overseas live link is allowed – I understand this to mean a scenario where one or even both parties to the process are not physically present in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This is consistent with the position under existing law.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There is an existing framework providing various options for overseas Singaporeans who need to make a statutory declaration or who need a document to be notarised.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For instance, they may approach a notary public in that country or seek assistance from a Singapore Overseas Mission.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For oaths, I mentioned earlier that our laws provide for oaths to be taken in a wide range of different processes and circumstances.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Requirements such as who must take an oath, who the oath must be taken before and the form of words that must be used are set out in those existing laws.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, apart from making clear that the use of the stipulated electronic modalities is acceptable, the Bills do not make changes to the frameworks under existing law.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Therefore, to Mr Yip's question on whether any specific oath can be taken when one or more persons involved in the process is physically outside Singapore, this is context specific and must be determined with reference to the legislation governing the process in question.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For example, in the case of a witness who is appearing before Court, it is possible under the rules governing court procedure for the witness to be overseas and to take his oath and give evidence to a Singapore Court through live video link.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: However, this will be subject to the grant of permission by the Court.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There are also existing rules and requirements on this in the Evidence Act and the Criminal Procedure Code.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Likewise, to Mr Dennis Tan's question on whether an oath may be administered en masse to polling or counting agents, this must also be determined with reference to the existing legislative provisions under the Parliamentary Elections Act and the Presidential Elections Act.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The amendments under these Bills do not change the existing position under these Acts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The manner in which oaths are administered for polling and counting agents – including whether video link is used in the first place – is something that the Elections Department will decide, depending on their assessment of what is most appropriate, to ensure that the integrity of the election process, as a whole, is not undermined.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Next, Mr Lim Biow Chuan asked whether consular officers may administer oaths and affirmations or perform notarial acts through virtual means.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The powers of a consular officer to administer an oath or affirmation, take an affidavit or perform a notarial act are set out in the Diplomatic and Consular Officers (Oaths and Fees) Act 1968, or the DCOA.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Today, consular officers only perform such functions in-person.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Together with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA), we are studying possible ways, including by electronic means, to address such difficulties.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Next, Mr Louis Ng asked several queries relating to interpreters.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Ng asked whether an interpreter has to be present in person with the client.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It is possible for the CFO or NP, client and interpreter to be at three separate physical locations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Ng asked what steps the CFO or NP should take to ensure that the interpretation and communication is accurately done.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Today, CFOs and NPs are already required to take steps to safeguard the integrity of the process when it is done in person.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Similar requirements will continue to apply under the electronic framework.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For example, CFOs and NPs may be required to ensure that they can hear and see both the client and the interpreter simultaneously.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The specific steps CFOs and NP will be required to take will be set out in either subsidiary legislation or in the refreshed guidelines to be issued by the Singapore Academy of Law.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Ultimately, however, it will be up to each individual CFO and NP to exercise their professional judgment and experience, to satisfy themselves that the contents of the relevant document have been properly interpreted.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: If the CFO or NP is, at any point in time, not satisfied with the integrity of the process, the CFO or NP should stop the process, and request that the statutory declaration or oath or affirmation, be made or taken physically in person instead.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Question is, "That the Bill be now read a Second time." Pursuant to Article 5(2) of the Constitution, a vote is taken to ascertain that the Second Reading of the Bill is supported by the votes of not less than two-thirds of the total number of Elected and Non-Constituency Members of Parliament, which is 60 Members.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Before I proceed to start the electronic voting, may I remind Members that they are to be seated at their designated seats and should only start to vote when the voting buttons on the arm rest start to blink.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members are advised to check that their names are registered according to their vote indication when the voting results are shown on the display screens.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Before I proceed to declare the results of the vote, are there any Members who wish to claim that his or her vote has not been displayed or displayed incorrectly on the screens?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Okay, Mr Desmond Choo, we will add that in.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Now, Sir, I beg to move, "That the Bill be now read a Third time."

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Question is, "That the Bill be now read a Third time." Pursuant to Article 5(2) of the Constitution, a vote is taken to ascertain that the Third Reading of the Bill is supported by the votes of not less than two-thirds of the total number of Elected and Non-Constituency Members of Parliament, which is 60 Members.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members are advised to check that their names are registered according to their vote indication when the voting results are shown on the display screens.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Before I proceed to declare the results of the vote, are there any Members who wish to claim that his or her vote has not been displayed or is displayed incorrectly on the screens?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will proceed to declare the voting results now.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: There are now 83 "Ayes"; zero "Noes"; zero "Abstentions".
